chapters.title: The reader Ḥamzah and his two transmitters
paragraphs: The reader: Ḥamzah ibn Ḥabīb al-Zayyāt al-Kūfī (80–156 AH) is the sixth of the seven readers. He learned the Qurʾān from Sulaymān al-Aʿmash, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq and others, and his reading reaches the Prophet through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd. After ʿĀṣim he became the leading reciter of Kūfah.
Khalaf: Khalaf ibn Hishām al-Bazzār al-Baghdādī, Abū Muḥammad (150–229 AH). He also has a qirāʾah of his own, counted as the tenth, separate from what he transmits from Ḥamzah.
Khallād: Abū ʿĪsā Khallād ibn Khālid al-Shaybānī al-Ṣayrafī al-Kūfī (died 220 AH).
Chain: Both transmitters took the reading from Sulaym ibn ʿĪsā, Ḥamzah's student, and they differ from each other in a small number of places.

Way of transmission: Everything below follows al-Shāṭibiyyah (Ḥirz al-Amānī of Imām al-Shāṭibī) and is described by comparison with Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim. In that poem fāʾ stands for Ḥamzah, ḍād for Khalaf and qāf for Khallād.

chapters.title: The basmalah and joining two surahs
paragraphs: Between two surahs: Ḥamzah, in both riwāyahs, has one way only: waṣl without the basmalah. The last word of the first surah keeps its vowel and is joined straight to the first word of the next, with whatever tajwīd rule arises between them. Ḥafṣ separates the surahs with the basmalah.

Starting a surah: When recitation begins at the head of a surah the basmalah is read, as all readers agree. It is also read between Sūrat al-Nās and Sūrat al-Fātiḥah. Ḥamzah counts the basmalah as the first āyah of al-Fātiḥah.
Al-Anfāl and al-Tawbah: As for every reader, there is no basmalah, and three ways are allowed: waqf, sakt or waṣl.
The four sakts of Ḥafṣ: Ḥamzah does not pause where Ḥafṣ makes his obligatory sakt, at عِوَجًا (18:1), مَرْقَدِنَا (36:52), مَن رَّاقٍ (75:27) and بَل رَّانَ (83:14); he reads straight through.

chapters.title: Sūrat al-Fātiḥah and the ishmām of ṣād
paragraphs: Maliki: Both transmitters read مَلِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ (1:4) without an alif after the mīm. Ḥafṣ reads مَالِكِ.
Khalaf: He reads the ṣād of الصِّرَاطَ and صِرَاطَ with ishmām wherever the word occurs in the Qurʾān. Ishmām here means mixing the ṣād with the sound of zāy, which gives a heavy sound close to ẓāʾ.

Khallād: He reads this ishmām only in the first occurrence, اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ in al-Fātiḥah. Everywhere else, including صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ in the next āyah, he reads a pure ṣād like Ḥafṣ.

Ṣād sākinah before dāl: Ḥamzah reads a sākin ṣād followed by dāl with the same ishmām, as in وَمَنْ أَصْدَقُ (4:87), يَصْدِفُونَ (6:46), تَصْدِيَةً (8:35), فَاصْدَعْ (15:94), قَصْدُ السَّبِيلِ (16:9), يُصْدِرَ (28:23) and تَصْدِيقَ (10:37, 12:111). Ḥafṣ reads a pure ṣād.
Al-muṣayṭirūn: The source also lists الْمُصَيْطِرُونَ (52:37) and بِمُصَيْطِرٍ (88:22) among the words read with ishmām.

chapters.title: Mīm al-jamʿ and the ḍammah of the hāʾ
paragraphs: Three words: Ḥamzah reads the hāʾ of عَلَيْهُمْ, إِلَيْهُمْ and لَدَيْهُمْ with ḍammah, in waṣl and in waqf. Ḥafṣ reads kasrah: عَلَيْهِمْ.
Before a vowelled letter: The mīm al-jamʿ stays sākin, with no ṣilah, as with Ḥafṣ: وَاجْتَبَيْنَاهُمْ وَهَدَيْنَاهُمْ (6:87).

Before a sākin: The mīm takes a passing ḍammah, without ṣilah, to avoid two sākins. When the hāʾ before it follows a kasrah or a sākin yāʾ, Ḥamzah reads the hāʾ with ḍammah as well, in waṣl: عَلَيْهُمُ الْقِتَالُ (2:246), بِهُمُ الْأَسْبَابُ (2:166), يُرِيهُمُ اللَّهُ (2:167). Ḥafṣ keeps the kasrah of the hāʾ: بِهِمُ الْأَسْبَابُ.
In waqf: When stopping on such a word the hāʾ returns to kasrah as with Ḥafṣ (بِهِمْ, يُرِيهِمْ); only the three words above keep their ḍammah.
Before hamzat al-qaṭʿ: Khalaf has two ways in waṣl, without sakt and with sakt on the mīm, as in عَلَيْهُمْ ءَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ (2:6). Khallād reads without sakt.

chapters.title: Hāʾ al-kināyah
paragraphs: General rule: As with Ḥafṣ, the pronoun hāʾ between two vowelled letters is lengthened by a wāw or yāʾ of two ḥarakāt. When hamzat al-qaṭʿ follows, this ṣilah becomes a madd munfaṣil and Ḥamzah lengthens it six ḥarakāt: مَالُهُ إِذَا (92:11).

Words read with sukūn: Ḥamzah reads the hāʾ sākin in يُؤَدِّهْ إِلَيْكَ (3:75, both), نُؤْتِهْ مِنْهَا (3:145, both, and 42:20), نُوَلِّهْ مَا تَوَلَّىٰ وَنُصْلِهْ جَهَنَّمَ (4:115) and فَأَلْقِهْ إِلَيْهُمْ (27:28). Ḥafṣ reads the first four words with kasrah and ṣilah, and agrees with him in فَأَلْقِهْ.

Wa-yattaqih (24:52): Khallād has two ways: sukūn of the hāʾ, وَيَتَّقِهْ, and kasrah with ṣilah, وَيَتَّقِهِ. The sukūn is transmitted for Khallād alone, which leaves Khalaf with the ṣilah. In both riwāyahs the qāf has kasrah; Ḥafṣ alone reads the qāf sākin, وَيَتَّقْهِ.
Yarḍah and arjih: يَرْضَهُ لَكُمْ (39:7) is read with a short ḍammah and no ṣilah, and أَرْجِهْ وَأَخَاهُ (7:111, 26:36) without a hamzah and with the hāʾ sākin. Ḥafṣ reads both the same way.
Two readings special to Ḥafṣ: Ḥamzah reads the hāʾ with kasrah in وَمَا أَنسَانِيهِ (18:63) and in عَلَيْهِ اللَّهَ (48:10), so the lām of the Name is thin after it. Ḥafṣ reads ḍammah in both.

chapters.title: Madd and qaṣr
paragraphs: Madd muttaṣil: When the hamzah follows the madd letter in the same word, Ḥamzah lengthens fully, six ḥarakāt (ṭūl): جَزَاؤُهُمْ عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ (98:8). Ḥafṣ reads a medium length.

Madd munfaṣil: When the madd letter ends one word and the hamzah begins the next, whether the two are written joined or apart, Ḥamzah again reads six ḥarakāt only: يَا أَيُّهَا, يَا أَهْلَ, هَٰؤُلَاءِ.

chapters.title: The hamzahs
paragraphs: Two hamzahs in one word: Ḥamzah pronounces both fully (taḥqīq), whatever the vowel of the second and with no alif between them: ءَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ (2:6), أَئِنَّا, أَءُنزِلَ (38:8).
Aʾaʿjamiyyun (41:44): He reads أَأَعْجَمِيٌّ with two full hamzahs. Ḥafṣ softens the second (tashīl).

An extra interrogative hamzah: Ḥamzah reads أَأَن كَانَ ذَا مَالٍ وَبَنِينَ (68:14) with two full hamzahs, where Ḥafṣ has one. He also adds the interrogative hamzah in أَءَامَنتُمْ (7:123, 20:71, 26:49): the first two hamzahs are full and the third is an alif of two ḥarakāt for every reader. Ḥafṣ reads ءَامَنتُمْ as a statement.

Hamzat al-waṣl after the interrogative: In ءَآلذَّكَرَيْنِ (6:143, 6:144), ءَآللَّهُ (10:59, 27:59) and ءَآلْآنَ (10:51, 10:91) he has the two ways of all readers: ibdāl of hamzat al-waṣl into an alif of six ḥarakāt, which is preferred, or tashīl.

Repeated question: In the eleven passages where a question is repeated, as in أَءِذَا كُنَّا تُرَابًا أَءِنَّا لَفِي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ (13:5), Ḥamzah reads both parts as questions with two hamzahs. He differs from Ḥafṣ in one place only: أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الْفَاحِشَةَ (29:28), which Ḥafṣ reads as a statement, إِنَّكُمْ.
Waṣl and waqf: This taḥqīq is for connected reading; when he stops on a word that contains a hamzah he lightens it, as described below.

chapters.title: Sakt before the hamzah
paragraphs: What it is: Sakt is a brief pause without breath on a sākin letter before a hamzah. Ḥafṣ has none of it.

Lām al-taʿrīf in waṣl: On the lām of the definite article before a hamzah, as in الْأَرْضِ, الْآخِرَةِ and الْإِنسَانُ, Khalaf makes sakt. Khallād has two ways: sakt, which is given first in performance, and reading without sakt like Ḥafṣ.
Shayʾ in waṣl: The same holds for شَيْءٍ and شَيْئًا, where the sakt falls on the sākin yāʾ: Khalaf makes sakt; Khallād has sakt and no sakt.

A sākin ending one word before a hamzah in the next: Here only Khalaf makes sakt, and with two ways: no sakt first, then sakt. Khallād reads without sakt. This covers a sound sākin, قَدْ أَفْلَحَ (23:1); a līn letter, خَلَوْا إِلَىٰ (2:14), ابْنَيْ ءَادَمَ (5:27); tanwīn, عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ; and mīm al-jamʿ, عَلَيْكُمْ أَنفُسَكُمْ (5:105). Khalaf's sakt comes by way of Abū al-Fatḥ Fāris, and his reading without it by way of Ṭāhir ibn Ghalbūn.

In waqf on the word carrying the hamzah: With lām al-taʿrīf Ḥamzah stops with naql or with sakt; plain taḥqīq is not allowed. On شَيْءٍ and شَيْئًا he stops with naql or with idghām. When the sākin is in the previous word he stops with naql first, then taḥqīq, and Khalaf adds sakt as a third way. After mīm al-jamʿ there is no naql: taḥqīq only, with sakt as well for Khalaf.

chapters.title: The waqf of Ḥamzah on the hamzah
paragraphs: Scope: When Ḥamzah stops on a word whose hamzah is in the middle or at the end, he lightens that hamzah. Khalaf and Khallād agree in this. Ḥafṣ never changes a hamzah in waqf.

The tools: Tashīl bayna bayna is a sound between the hamzah and the madd letter of its own vowel. Ibdāl turns the hamzah into the madd letter that suits the vowel before it. Naql moves the hamzah's vowel to the sākin before it and drops the hamzah. Ḥadhf drops the hamzah.

Two approaches: Takhfīf qiyāsī follows the grammatical rule of the hamzah and is the method of al-Shāṭibī. Takhfīf rasmī follows the way the hamzah is written in the muṣḥaf, as transmitted from al-Dānī and Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and uses ibdāl and ḥadhf.

Sākin hamzah after a vowel: Ibdāl into the madd letter of the preceding vowel: يُؤْمِنُونَ becomes يُومِنُونَ, يَأْكُلُ becomes يَاكُلُ, الذِّئْبُ becomes الذِّيبُ, اقْرَأْ becomes اقْرَا. The same applies after a prefix (فَأْتُوا becomes فَاتُوا) and when the hamzah opens a word joined to the vowel before it: الَّذِي اؤْتُمِنَ (2:283) is read الَّذِيتُمِنَ.

Final vowelled hamzah after a vowel: The stop makes it sākin, so it is replaced in the same way: الْمَلَأُ becomes الْمَلَا, بَدَأَ becomes بَدَا, يَسْتَهْزِئُ becomes يَسْتَهْزِي, امْرُؤٌ becomes امْرُو. If the hamzah had fatḥah this is the only way. If it had kasrah or ḍammah, tashīl with rawm is added.

Riʾyan, tuʾwī and ruʾyā: In وَرِءْيًا (19:74), تُؤْوِي (33:51) and تُؤْوِيهِ (70:13) the replacing yāʾ or wāw meets its like, and Ḥamzah has two ways: keeping the two letters apart, or merging them (رِيًّا, تُوِّي). In رُؤْيَاكَ, الرُّؤْيَا and رُؤْيَايَ in Sūrat Yūsuf the hamzah becomes a wāw (رُويَا), which may also be turned into yāʾ and merged (رُيَّا).
Anbiʾhum: In أَنبِئْهُمْ (2:33) and وَنَبِّئْهُمْ (15:51, 54:28) the hamzah becomes yāʾ, and the hāʾ after it may keep its ḍammah or take kasrah: أَنبِيهُمْ or أَنبِيهِمْ.

Vowelled hamzah after a sound sākin: Naql. Its vowel moves to the sākin and the hamzah drops: الْقُرْءَانُ becomes الْقُرَانُ, مَسْئُولًا becomes مَسُولًا, يَسْأَلُونَ becomes يَسَلُونَ. The same is done with lām al-taʿrīf (الْأَرْضِ becomes الَرْضِ), with a sākin ending the previous word (قَدْ أَفْلَحَ becomes قَدَ افْلَحَ), with a līn letter (خَلَوْا إِلَىٰ becomes خَلَوِ الَىٰ) and with tanwīn (عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ). Naql is never made to mīm al-jamʿ or to a madd letter.

Final hamzah after a sound sākin: After naql the word is stopped according to the vowel that moved. From a fatḥah: sukūn only, as in الْخَبْءَ (27:25). From a kasrah: sukūn or rawm, as in الْمَرْءِ. From a ḍammah: sukūn, rawm or ishmām, as in دِفْءٌ (16:5) and مِلْءُ (3:91).
Hamzah in the middle after alif: Tashīl bayna bayna, with the alif read either long (six ḥarakāt) or short (two): جَاءَهُمْ, الْمَلَائِكَةُ, ءَابَاؤُكُمْ.

Final hamzah after alif: The hamzah is replaced by an alif, with three lengths allowed: two, four or six ḥarakāt. With a fatḥah these three are all there is: جَاءَ, الدِّمَاءَ. With a kasrah or ḍammah two more are added, tashīl with rawm on the long madd and on the short, making five ways: السَّمَاءِ, يَشَاءُ, السُّفَهَاءُ.

After an added wāw or yāʾ: When the wāw or yāʾ before the hamzah is not a root letter (patterns such as faʿīl and fuʿūl), the hamzah is turned into its like and the two are merged: خَطِيئَتُهُ becomes خَطِيَّتُهُ, هَنِيئًا becomes هَنِيًّا, بَرِيئُونَ becomes بَرِيُّونَ. At the end of a word the doubled letter is stopped with sukūn or rawm for a kasrah, قُرُوءٍ (2:228), and with sukūn, rawm or ishmām for a ḍammah, النَّسِيءُ (9:37). Ibdāl without idghām is not allowed.

After a root wāw or yāʾ: Two methods are allowed, naql and ibdāl with idghām: شَيْئًا is read شَيَا or شَيَّا, سَوْءَةَ is read سَوَةَ or سَوَّةَ, سِيئَتْ is read سِيَتْ or سِيَّتْ. At the end of a word each method takes the stops its vowel allows: two ways for a fatḥah, السُّوءَ; four for a kasrah, شَيْءٍ; six for a ḍammah, الْمُسِيءُ (40:58), لَتَنُوءُ (28:76).

Vowelled hamzah after a vowel, ibdāl: A hamzah with fatḥah after a kasrah becomes a yāʾ with fatḥah: فِئَةٍ becomes فِيَةٍ, خَاطِئَةٍ becomes خَاطِيَةٍ. A hamzah with fatḥah after a ḍammah becomes a wāw with fatḥah: يُؤَيِّدُ becomes يُوَيِّدُ, مُؤَجَّلًا becomes مُوَجَّلًا.

Vowelled hamzah after a vowel, tashīl: In the other seven combinations of vowels the hamzah is read with tashīl bayna bayna: سَأَلَ, يَوْمَئِذٍ, خَاسِئِينَ, بِرُءُوسِكُمْ, يَكْلَؤُكُمْ, سُئِلُوا, سَنُقْرِئُكَ. Al-Akhfash replaced a hamzah with ḍammah after kasrah by yāʾ (سَنُقْرِيُكَ) and one with kasrah after ḍammah by wāw (سُوِلُوا); the source prefers tashīl in both.

Ḥadhf by the rasm: A hamzah with ḍammah that has no seat in the script, comes after a kasrah and is followed by a wāw of madd may be dropped, and the letter before the wāw then takes ḍammah: مُسْتَهْزِءُونَ becomes مُسْتَهْزُونَ, مُتَّكِئُونَ becomes مُتَّكُونَ, لِيُطْفِئُوا becomes لِيُطْفُوا. Keeping the kasrah after dropping the hamzah is rejected.

Ibdāl by the rasm: Where the hamzah is written on a wāw or a yāʾ, a stop on that letter is transmitted in particular words, such as تَفْتَؤُا (12:85) and يَتَفَيَّؤُا (16:48). This rests on transmission and is not general: in words like نِسَاؤُكُمْ, خَائِفِينَ, الْمَلَائِكَةِ and يُرَاءُونَ only tashīl is read.

Hamzah made medial by a prefix: When a hamzah that begins a word comes to stand in the middle because a particle is attached, Ḥamzah stops with two ways: taḥqīq, and the lightening its vowels call for. That is tashīl in ءَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ, سَأَصْرِفُ, فَإِذَا, كَأَنَّهُمْ and وَأَنتُمْ, and ibdāl into yāʾ in بِأَنَّهُمْ and لِأَبَوَيْهِ. After hāʾ al-tanbīh and yāʾ al-nidāʾ (هَا أَنتُمْ, يَا أَيُّهَا) he reads taḥqīq with full madd, or tashīl with long or short madd.

Counted examples: هَٰؤُلَاءِ is stopped in thirteen ways: taḥqīq with madd, tashīl with madd or tashīl with qaṣr for the first hamzah, each with the five ways of the last, less the two pairings where the two tashīls would differ in length. قُلْ أَؤُنَبِّئُكُم (3:15) has twelve: naql, taḥqīq or sakt for the first hamzah, taḥqīq or tashīl for the second, ibdāl or tashīl for the third. ءَآلْآنَ (10:51, 10:91) has fifteen.

chapters.title: Idghām and iẓhār
paragraphs: Dhāl of idh: Khalaf merges it into tāʾ and dāl only, as in إِذ تَّمْشِي (20:40) and إِذ دَّخَلُوا (15:52), and reads iẓhār before zāy, ṣād, sīn and jīm. Khallād merges it into five letters, tāʾ, dāl, zāy, ṣād and sīn, as in وَإِذ زَّيَّنَ (8:48), وَإِذ صَّرَفْنَا (46:29) and إِذ سَّمِعْتُمُوهُ (24:12), and reads iẓhār before jīm only. Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār before all six.

Dāl of qad: Ḥamzah merges it into all eight of its letters: sīn, dhāl, ḍād, ẓāʾ, zāy, jīm, ṣād and shīn. Examples: قَد سَّمِعَ (58:1), وَلَقَد ذَّرَأْنَا (7:179), قَد شَّغَفَهَا (12:30). Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār.

Tāʾ al-taʾnīth: Ḥamzah merges the sākin feminine tāʾ into all six of its letters: sīn, thāʾ, ṣād, zāy, ẓāʾ and jīm. Examples: كَذَّبَت ثَّمُودُ (26:141), حَصِرَت صُّدُورُهُمْ (4:90), نَضِجَت جُّلُودُهُمْ (4:56). Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār.

Lām of hal and bal: Ḥamzah merges it into sīn, tāʾ and thāʾ: بَل سَّوَّلَتْ (12:18), هَل تَّرَىٰ (67:3), هَل ثُّوِّبَ (83:36). Khallād also has idghām, beside iẓhār, in بَل طَّبَعَ (4:155). Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār.
Agreed idghām: As with every reader, the dhāl of idh merges into ẓāʾ, the dāl of qad into tāʾ, the feminine tāʾ into dāl and ṭāʾ, and the lām of hal, bal and qul into rāʾ.

Bāʾ before fāʾ: Khallād merges the jussive bāʾ into fāʾ in five places: أَوْ يَغْلِب فَّسَوْفَ (4:74), وَإِن تَعْجَب فَّعَجَبٌ (13:5), اذْهَب فَّمَن (17:63), فَاذْهَب فَّإِنَّ (20:97) and وَمَن لَّمْ يَتُب فَّأُولَٰئِكَ (49:11). In the last he has iẓhār as well. Khalaf reads iẓhār in all five.
Irkab maʿanā (11:42): Khallād has two ways in ارْكَب مَّعَنَا, idghām of the bāʾ into the mīm and iẓhār.

Yuʿadhdhib man (2:284): Ḥamzah reads فَيَغْفِرْ لِمَن يَشَاءُ وَيُعَذِّب مَّن يَشَاءُ with both verbs in the jussive and the bāʾ merged into the mīm. Ḥafṣ reads both verbs with ḍammah and so has no idghām.
Dhāl into tāʾ: Ḥamzah merges in عُذتُّ (40:27, 44:20), فَنَبَذتُّهَا (20:96) and every form of اتَّخَذتُّمْ and أَخَذتُّمْ, singular or plural, such as لَئِنِ اتَّخَذتَّ (26:29). Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār.
Thāʾ into tāʾ: Ḥamzah merges in أُورِثتُّمُوهَا (7:43, 43:72) and in لَبِثتَّ and لَبِثتُّمْ wherever they occur. Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār.

Other single places: Ḥamzah merges the dāl of the letter ṣād into the dhāl in كٓهيعٓصٓ ذِّكْرُ (19:1–2), the dāl into thāʾ in يُرِد ثَّوَابَ (3:145), and the thāʾ into dhāl in يَلْهَث ذَّٰلِكَ (7:176).

Opening letters: Ḥamzah reads iẓhār of the nūn in يسٓ وَالْقُرْآنِ (36:1–2), where he also reads the yāʾ with imālah, and in نٓ وَالْقَلَمِ (68:1), like Ḥafṣ. He also reads iẓhār of the nūn of sīn before the mīm in طسٓمٓ (26:1, 28:1), where Ḥafṣ merges.

Idghām kabīr: Ḥamzah merges a vowelled tāʾ into the next letter in وَالصَّافَّات صَّفًّا, فَالزَّاجِرَات زَّجْرًا, فَالتَّالِيَات ذِّكْرًا (37:1–3) and وَالذَّارِيَات ذَّرْوًا (51:1), with a madd of six ḥarakāt before it and without rawm. He also merges in بَيَّت طَّائِفَةٌ (4:81) and reads أَتُمِدُّونِّي (27:36) with one doubled nūn.
Khallād's idghām kabīr: Khallād has two ways, idghām and iẓhār, in فَالْمُلْقِيَات ذِّكْرًا (77:5) and فَالْمُغِيرَات صُّبْحًا (100:3). Khalaf reads iẓhār in both.

chapters.title: Nūn sākinah and tanwīn
paragraphs: Wāw and yāʾ: Khalaf merges the nūn sākinah and tanwīn into wāw and yāʾ completely, without ghunnah: مِن وَّاقٍ (13:34), مِن يَّوْمِهِمُ (51:60). Khallād keeps the ghunnah, like Ḥafṣ and the other readers.
Limit: This idghām occurs only between two words. Inside one word the nūn is read clearly by all: دُنْيَا, صِنْوَانٌ, قِنْوَانٌ, بُنْيَانٌ.

chapters.title: Fatḥ, imālah and taqlīl
paragraphs: Terms: Imālah bends the alif about halfway toward yāʾ. Taqlīl is a lesser bend, between imālah and fatḥ. Fatḥ is the plain open alif, which Ḥafṣ reads in all the words below except مَجْرَاهَا (11:41).

Alif from yāʾ: Ḥamzah reads imālah in every final alif that comes from an original yāʾ, in nouns and verbs: الْهُدَىٰ, تَوَلَّىٰ, كَفَىٰ, أَدْنَىٰ. The origin shows in the dual of a noun (فَتَىٰ, فَتَيَانِ) and in the first person of a verb (نَادَىٰ, نَادَيْتُ).

Feminine alif: He reads imālah in the alif of the patterns faʿlā, fiʿlā and fuʿlā, as in الدُّنْيَا, التَّقْوَىٰ, إِحْدَىٰ, مُوسَىٰ, عِيسَىٰ, يَحْيَىٰ, and of fuʿālā and faʿālā, as in كُسَالَىٰ and الْيَتَامَىٰ.

Alif written as yāʾ: He reads imālah in words of unknown origin written with yāʾ, such as أَنَّىٰ, مَتَىٰ, عَسَىٰ, بَلَىٰ and يَا وَيْلَتَىٰ. Five words written so are excluded and read with fatḥ: لَدَى, عَلَى, إِلَى, حَتَّىٰ and مَا زَكَىٰ (24:21).

Alif from wāw: Three-letter words whose alif comes from wāw are read with fatḥ: دَعَا, عَفَا, نَجَا, دَنَا, عَلَا, الصَّفَا, شَفَا, عَصَا. Once such a verb gains an extra letter its alif goes back to yāʾ and takes imālah: أَنجَىٰ, زَكَّاهَا, ابْتَلَىٰ. He also reads imālah in الضُّحَىٰ, ضُحَاهَا, الرِّبَا and الْقُوَىٰ.

Aḥyā and a few others: Ḥamzah reads imālah in أَحْيَا only when a wāw precedes it, وَأَحْيَا (53:44); otherwise fatḥ. He reads imālah in هَدَانِي, تُقَاةً (3:28), مُزْجَاةٍ (12:88), الْحَوَايَا (6:146), إِنَاهُ (33:53), كِلَاهُمَا (17:23), رَمَىٰ (8:17) and both occurrences of أَعْمَىٰ in 17:72.

Verse endings: He reads imālah in the final alifs suited to it at the ends of the āyāt of eleven surahs: Ṭā-Hā, al-Najm, al-Maʿārij, al-Qiyāmah, al-Nāziʿāt, ʿAbasa, al-Aʿlā, al-Shams, al-Layl, al-Ḍuḥā and al-ʿAlaq.
Alif after rāʾ: He reads imālah in every final alif written as yāʾ after a rāʾ: تَرَىٰ, أُخْرَىٰ, الْقُرَىٰ, ذِكْرَىٰ, بُشْرَىٰ, النَّصَارَىٰ, مَجْرَاهَا.

Before a sākin: When the alif drops in waṣl because a sākin follows, there is no imālah; it returns when he stops on the word. This applies before a sākin in the next word, as in مُوسَى الْكِتَابَ and عِيسَى ابْنِ مَرْيَمَ, and to words ending in tanwīn, such as هُدًى, مُصَلًّى, سُوًى (20:58) and سُدًى (75:36).

Raʾā: Before a vowelled letter he reads imālah of both the rāʾ and the hamzah: رَأَىٰ كَوْكَبًا (6:76), رَآهُ مُسْتَقِرًّا (27:40). Before a sākin, as in رَأَى الْقَمَرَ (6:77) and رَأَى الشَّمْسَ (6:78), he reads imālah of the rāʾ alone in waṣl.
Tarāʾā (26:61): In تَرَاءَى الْجَمْعَانِ he reads imālah of the rāʾ alone in waṣl. Stopping on تَرَاءَى, he reads imālah of both the rāʾ and the hamzah, with tashīl of the hamzah.
Naʾā: In وَنَأَىٰ بِجَانِبِهِ (17:83, 41:51) Khalaf reads imālah of both the nūn and the hamzah. Khallād reads imālah of the hamzah only.

The ten verbs: He reads imālah of the middle alif in ten three-letter past-tense verbs in all their forms: جَاءَ, شَاءَ, زَادَ, خَابَ, طَابَ, ضَاقَ, حَاقَ, خَافَ, زَاغَ and رَانَ (83:14). The form زَاغَتْ is excluded, and so is anything that is not a three-letter past verb, such as يَخَافُونَ, ضَائِقٌ and أَزَاغَ.

Taqlīl: Ḥamzah reads taqlīl in الْبَوَارِ (14:28) and الْقَهَّارِ, where the alif precedes a final rāʾ with kasrah, and in التَّوْرَاةَ wherever it occurs. He also reads taqlīl in an alif between two rāʾs when the second is final and has kasrah: الْأَبْرَارِ (83:18), دَارُ الْقَرَارِ, مِنَ الْأَشْرَارِ (38:62).
Ḍiʿāfan and ātīka: Khalaf reads imālah in ضِعَافًا (4:9) and in أَنَا ءَاتِيكَ بِهِ (27:39, 27:40). Khallād has two ways in these places, imālah and fatḥ.

chapters.title: Waqf with rawm and ishmām
paragraphs: Ways of stopping: Sukūn is the basic stop. Ḥamzah is among the readers who also stop with rawm, a faint part of the vowel in a lowered voice, and with ishmām, a silent rounding of the lips after the sukūn. Rawm is used on a ḍammah and a kasrah, ishmām on a ḍammah only; neither is used on a fatḥah or on an original sukūn.
After ibdāl: A madd letter that has replaced a hamzah is sākin, so it is stopped with plain sukūn: الْمَلَأُ as الْمَلَا, يَشَأْ as يَشَا, لُؤْلُؤٌ as لُولُو.

After naql and idghām: The letter that received a hamzah's ḍammah or kasrah by naql, as in دِفْءٌ, and the wāw or yāʾ doubled by idghām, as in قُرُوءٍ and شَيْءٍ, may take rawm, and ishmām too when the vowel is ḍammah.
Tashīl with rawm: A final hamzah with ḍammah or kasrah that follows a vowel or an alif may be read with tashīl together with rawm: يَشَاءُ, الْمَلَأُ, يُبْدِئُ.
Rejected ways: Never using rawm at all, and using rawm or ishmām on a fatḥah, are both counted as irregular.

chapters.title: Yāʾāt al-iḍāfah
paragraphs: What they are: The yāʾ of the first person attached to a noun, a verb or a particle, as in بَيْتِيَ and إِنِّي. It is not a root letter and is written in the muṣḥaf. The readers differ over reading it with fatḥah or with sukūn in 212 places, grouped by what follows the yāʾ: hamzat al-qaṭʿ with fatḥah, kasrah or ḍammah, and hamzat al-waṣl with or without lām al-taʿrīf.

Before lām al-taʿrīf: Ḥamzah reads the yāʾ sākin in all fourteen places of this kind, so in waṣl it drops before the sākin lām: رَبِّي الَّذِي (2:258), مَسَّنِي الضُّرُّ (21:83), عِبَادِي الصَّالِحُونَ (21:105). In nine of the fourteen he is alone in this. Ḥafṣ reads the yāʾ with fatḥah in all of them except عَهْدِي الظَّالِمِينَ (2:124).

chapters.title: Yāʾāt al-zawāʾid
paragraphs: Rule: An extra yāʾ is a final yāʾ left out of the script of the muṣḥaf, which the readers differ over pronouncing. Ḥamzah drops all of them except two.
Atumiddūnnī (27:36): He reads the yāʾ in both waṣl and waqf, with the two nūns merged: أَتُمِدُّونِّي بِمَالٍ. Ḥafṣ reads أَتُمِدُّونَنِ with two nūns and no yāʾ.

Duʿāʾ (14:40): He reads the yāʾ in waṣl only: وَتَقَبَّلْ دُعَائِي رَبَّنَا. When stopping he drops it and stops on دُعَاءِ with the five ways of a final hamzah after alif. Ḥafṣ drops it in both states.

chapters.title: Notable individual words
paragraphs: Hāʾ al-sakt: In waṣl Ḥamzah drops the hāʾ of pause in لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ (2:259), فَبِهُدَاهُمُ اقْتَدِهْ (6:90), مَالِيَهْ (69:28), سُلْطَانِيَهْ (69:29) and مَا هِيَهْ (101:10), and keeps it when stopping. Ḥafṣ keeps it in both states.

Huzʾan and kufʾan: In waṣl he reads هُزْءًا and كُفْءًا (112:4) with a sākin middle letter and a hamzah; Ḥafṣ reads هُزُوًا and كُفُوًا. In waqf he has two ways: turning the hamzah into wāw, هُزْوَا and كُفْوَا, or naql, هُزَا and كُفَا.
Tarjiʿu: He reads تَرْجِعُ الْأُمُورُ with fatḥah on the tāʾ, where Ḥafṣ reads تُرْجَعُ.

Umm after kasrah or yāʾ: In فَلِإِمِّهِ (4:11, both) he reads the hamzah with kasrah in waṣl and waqf. In فِي إِمِّ الْكِتَابِ (43:4) and فِي إِمِّهَا (28:59) he reads it with kasrah in waṣl only. Ḥafṣ reads ḍammah throughout.

Ummahātikum: In waṣl he reads both the hamzah and the mīm with kasrah in بُطُونِ إِمِّهَاتِكُمْ (16:78, 39:6, 53:32) and بِيُوتِ إِمِّهَاتِكُمْ (24:61). When starting from the word itself, here and in the two words before, he reads ḍammah on the hamzah and fatḥah on the mīm like everyone.
Raʾūf: He reads رَؤُفٌ short, with no wāw after the hamzah, as in لَرَؤُفٌ رَّحِيمٌ (2:143). Ḥafṣ reads رَءُوفٌ.
Khuṭwāt and yā bunayyi: He reads خُطْوَاتِ with a sākin ṭāʾ and يَا بُنَيِّ with kasrah on the yāʾ wherever they occur. Ḥafṣ reads خُطُوَاتِ and يَا بُنَيَّ.
Kasrah on the first letter: He reads kasrah in place of Ḥafṣ's ḍammah in بِيُوتًا, الْبِيُوتَ, عِيُونًا, شِيُوخًا, الْغِيُوبِ and جِيُوبِهِنَّ.
Other listed words: The source also lists لَمَسْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ without an alif after the lām, تُمَاسُّوهُنَّ with an alif after the mīm, جَبْرَئِيلَ and مِيكَائِيلَ.

doubts: Istiʿādhah: the primary source has no section on it, so nothing is stated.

Mīm al-jamʿ before a sākin: the primary source's English only says the mīm takes a passing ḍammah; the ḍammah of the hāʾ in waṣl (عَلَيْهُمُ الْقِتَالُ, بِهُمُ الْأَسْبَابُ) and its return to kasrah in waqf are taken from the Shāṭibiyyah line it quotes and from rules-of-the-10-qiraat.txt.
Al-muṣayṭirūn (52:37) and bi-muṣayṭir (88:22): the source only lists them among the ishmām words and does not say whether Khalaf and Khallād differ.

Wa-yattaqih (24:52): the source gives sukūn with khulf for Khallād only; Khalaf's kasrah with ṣilah is inferred, not stated. The source also shows فِيهِ مُهَانًا (25:69) next to Ḥafṣ's special words without saying how Ḥamzah reads it, so it is left out.

Lām of hal and bal: in the extracted text the third letter of Ḥamzah's idghām is garbled; thāʾ is taken from the Shāṭibiyyah line quoted and the example هَل ثُّوِّبَ. The source does not say outright that he reads iẓhār before the remaining letters.
Irkab maʿanā (11:42): the source gives Khallād's two ways only; Khalaf's reading is not stated.

Waqf on a hamzah with ḍammah after kasrah or kasrah after ḍammah: the source says no reader followed al-Akhfash's ibdāl here, yet its own count for قُلْ أَؤُنَبِّئُكُم includes ibdāl of the last hamzah. Both statements are reported as found.
Ibdāl by the rasm: the source lists the words written with wāw or yāʾ but does not spell out how each is pronounced in waqf; only the general principle is given.
Pages 56–63 (the summary of the waqf of Ḥamzah) and the detail on page 65 are diagrams with no extracted text, so nothing from them is included.

Yāʾāt al-iḍāfah: the primary source gives only the definition and the categories. The rule for the fourteen places before lām al-taʿrīf comes from rules-of-the-10-qiraat.txt; Ḥamzah's readings in the other categories are not stated here.
Taqlīl of الْقَرَارِ: the source places دَارُ الْقَرَارِ in Sūrat Ibrāhīm, but that phrase is in Ghāfir 40:39, so no reference is given.

Hāʾ al-sakt: the source says Ḥamzah drops it in waṣl in all seven places, including كِتَابِيَهْ and حِسَابِيَهْ in al-Ḥāqqah. Those two are left out because the Shāṭibiyyah transmission known for Ḥamzah covers only the five listed; this needs checking.
Tarjiʿu: the source writes يرجعون / ترجعون / ترجع الأمور with fatḥah without saying which places; only تَرْجِعُ الْأُمُورُ is stated here.

The source lists ولا, الريح, يبشر and جزءا among Ḥamzah's special words with no explanation; they are omitted. لَمَسْتُمُ, تُمَاسُّوهُنَّ, جَبْرَئِيلَ and مِيكَائِيلَ are vowelled from the letter forms shown, without an explanation in the source.
